questions.question: What is the CAP theorem and how does it affect real system design decisions?
questions.title: CAP Theorem: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: The CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response). In practice, partitions are inevitable, so the real choice is CP (reject requests during partition to stay consistent) or AP (serve potentially stale data to stay available). Most systems are not purely one or the other — they make different trade-offs per feature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands CAP as a practical design trade-off, not just a theoretical label
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating CAP as 'pick 2 of 3' — you cannot sacrifice partition tolerance in a distributed system, partitions happen whether you like it or not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss PACELC (extends CAP to normal operation: latency vs consistency when there is no partition) and per-feature trade-off decisions

sections.title: The Problem With How Most People Learn CAP
sections.content:
CAP theorem says a distributed system can guarantee at most two of three properties: **Consistency** (every read returns the latest write), **Availability** (every request gets a response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system works despite network splits between nodes). Most candidates describe it as "pick 2 of 3" and stop there. This is where the common mistake lives.

In any real distributed system, **you cannot sacrifice partition tolerance**. Networks fail — switches die, cables get cut, cloud availability zones lose connectivity. Partition tolerance isn't optional; it's a fact of distributed computing. So the real choice is between **CP** (consistent but temporarily unavailable during partitions) and **AP** (available but temporarily inconsistent during partitions).

The deeper insight: CAP only describes behavior **during a network partition**, which is a rare event. Most of the time, your system isn't partitioned, and the relevant trade-off is between **latency and consistency** — this is what the **PACELC** extension captures. Even when everything is working fine, choosing strong consistency means higher latency (because writes must propagate to replicas before acknowledging), while choosing availability means lower latency but stale reads.

sections.title: CP vs AP in Real Systems: What the Labels Actually Mean
sections.content:
The theory becomes useful only when mapped to real databases and the specific guarantees they make.

| System | CAP Classification | During Partition | Normal Operation | Use When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PostgreSQL** (single node) | CA (not distributed) | N/A — single node can't partition | Strong consistency, full availability | You don't need distribution |
| **PostgreSQL** (sync replication) | CP | Writes block until replica confirms; unavailable if replica is down | Consistent, higher write latency | Financial data, inventory counts |
| **Cassandra** | AP (tunable) | Accepts writes on all nodes; reconciles later | Tunable per query: `ONE` (fast, stale) to `ALL` (slow, consistent) | High-write workloads, geo-distributed |
| **MongoDB** | CP (default) | Primary election blocks writes for 10–30 seconds | Strong reads from primary, eventual from secondaries | Document workloads needing consistency |
| **DynamoDB** | AP (default) | Eventual consistency; strong consistency optional per-read | Eventually consistent by default, ~1ms reads | High availability, global tables |
| **CockroachDB** | CP | Ranges without quorum become unavailable | Serializable consistency via Raft consensus | Distributed SQL with strong guarantees |

The key takeaway: **most databases let you tune the trade-off per query**, not just at the system level. Cassandra's `QUORUM` consistency level gives you CP behavior for critical reads while keeping AP for others. DynamoDB offers consistent reads at 2× the cost. The "pick 2" framing is too rigid — real systems operate on a **consistency spectrum**.

sections.title: PACELC: The Extension That Actually Guides Design Decisions
sections.content:
CAP tells you what happens during a partition. **PACELC** (proposed by Daniel Abadi, 2012) extends the framework to cover normal operation, which is where your system spends 99.99% of its time.

PACELC reads: "If there is a **P**artition, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency. **E**lse, when operating normally, choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency."

| System | During Partition (PAC) | Normal Operation (ELC) | In Practice |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cassandra** | PA — accepts writes everywhere | EL — tunes for low latency by default | Fast writes, reconcile later |
| **MongoDB** | PC — primary election blocks writes | EC — reads from primary are consistent | Consistent but slower failover |
| **DynamoDB** | PA — all regions accept writes | EL — eventual consistency default | Ultra-fast, eventually consistent |
| **CockroachDB** | PC — quorum required for availability | EC — Raft consensus adds latency | Strong consistency, higher latency |

This matters because most design decisions aren't about partitions. They're about whether you're willing to pay **2–10ms extra latency per write** for strong consistency during normal operation. A payment system says yes — correctness matters more than speed. A social media feed says no — showing a post 500ms late is invisible to users, but adding 10ms to every read at 100K QPS is a real cost.

sections.title: Practical Verdict: How to Apply CAP in Design Interviews
sections.content:
**The framework for answering CAP questions in interviews:**

1. **Acknowledge that partition tolerance is not optional** — this immediately shows you understand the theorem beyond "pick 2"
2. **Frame it as CP vs AP** — the real choice is consistency during partitions (writes block) vs availability during partitions (writes accepted, reconcile later)
3. **Extend to PACELC** — mention that during normal operation, the trade-off is latency vs consistency, which is the decision you actually make day-to-day
4. **Map to the specific system** — name real databases and their classifications

**My decision rule:** choose **CP** for anything involving money, inventory, or permissions — correctness is non-negotiable. Choose **AP** for user-facing reads where staleness is tolerable (feeds, recommendations, analytics). Most production systems use both: a CP database for the source of truth and an AP cache or read store for serving traffic at low latency.

The strongest signal in an interview is showing that CAP isn't a binary choice but a **per-operation decision**. A single application can use `QUORUM` reads for checkout (CP) and `ONE` reads for browsing (AP), making the trade-off at the query level rather than the system level.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CP or AP is the real choice — not CA** — network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems; CA means "single node" in practice.
- **PACELC extends CAP to normal operations** — even without a partition, you trade latency for consistency on every write.
- **Strong vs eventual is a per-operation decision** — bank balances require strong consistency; shopping cart contents tolerate eventual.
- **Cassandra is AP by default, tunable** — `QUORUM` reads/writes give CP-like behavior at latency cost; `ONE` gives AP with eventual consistency.
- **Leader election timeout determines partition behavior** — a 30-second leader timeout means 30 seconds of unavailability on split.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read returns the most recent write), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition tolerance (the system continues operating despite network splits between nodes). In practice, network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, so the real choice is between CP and AP.

**CP systems — consistency over availability during splits:**
- When a network partition occurs, a CP system stops accepting writes rather than risk serving inconsistent data; ZooKeeper, HBase, and etcd make this trade
- The right choice for financial transactions, inventory counts, and any domain where showing incorrect data is worse than showing no data
- Strong consistency typically means synchronous replication — every write waits for replica acknowledgment, adding network round-trip latency to every write

**AP systems — availability over consistency during splits:**
- When a partition occurs, an AP system continues serving requests from all nodes, accepting that data may diverge; Cassandra, DynamoDB, and CouchDB make this trade
- Diverged data is reconciled later through conflict resolution (last-write-wins, vector clocks, application-specific merge)
- The right choice for shopping carts, user profiles, social feeds — domains where serving slightly stale data is better than returning an error

**PACELC extends CAP to normal operation:**
- Even without a partition, every distributed system trades latency for consistency on every write; synchronous replication gives consistency at the cost of latency; async replication reduces latency at the cost of potential stale reads
- This trade exists even when the network is healthy — understanding it prevents surprises when the system behaves differently under load

I recommend thinking per-operation rather than per-system: bank balance writes need CP consistency; product catalog reads tolerate AP eventual consistency; mixing strategies within one system is the correct and common production pattern.
